title: scholar-search MCP tools
description: Generated from the running server by scripts/dump-tools.py; do not edit by hand. scripts/dump-tools.py --check runs in the tests, in release-check and in CI, and fails when this file is stale.

tools.name: search
tools.description:
Search a channel for bibliographic records. Read-only.

channel: "cnki" (default; Chinese literature, Chinese queries) or
"webofscience" (English literature; also accepts a Web of Science expression
such as TS=(ionic AND actuator) AND PY=(2021-2026) — with no year range the
last five years are applied inside the expression).

Returns a shortlist by default: abstracts are omitted unless
include_abstract is true, and sort_by / min_citations / sources_only filter
locally without any browser action. For the full record call detail(url), which
infers the channel from the URL.

**Whether `detail` is free depends on the channel.** A Web of Science search
captures full records, so a following `detail` is served from the cache at no
cost; a CNKI search captures only the list, so the first `detail` for a record
still needs one network action. Asking twice for the same record is always
free.

An empty records list is a normal answer, not a failure: read `total` and
`dropped_year` before concluding that a topic has no papers.

**To get more records, the channel decides which lever exists.** Web of
Science has `exclude_ut`: pass back the UT values you already have (the last
segment of each record's `url`) and the same query returns the records you
have not seen. Do that rather than asking for a deeper `page` — each
exclusion call is one independent request, while each page turn re-submits the
query and keeps a result list open. CNKI has no exclusion field, so `page` is
how you go further there.

**`total` is the site's count for the query, before any local filter.** With
a year range applied, `total: 363` alongside nine records does NOT mean
"363 papers in that year" — it means the site matched 363 and this page lost
11 of its 20 to the year filter. `filters.year_scope: "page"` says so
explicitly, and `filters.dropped.year` gives the count. To get a year-accurate
total, put the year in the query (`PY=(2026)` on Web of Science,
`SU='x' and 年='2026'` on CNKI) or use `site_sort=date` and read the newest
page. `empty_reason: "all_dropped_by_year"` is the case where the whole page
was filtered away.

min_impact_factor is honoured by channels that ship journal metrics
(currently webofscience); records whose journal has no metric are dropped,
which lowers recall by design.

Two parameters sort and they are not interchangeable:

* `site_sort` (`relevance` / `date` / `citation`) asks the site to re-sort.
  That is two extra clicks and costs quota.
* `local_sort` (`none` / `citations` / `year`) re-orders the page already in
  hand: free, no browser action, no quota.

**Which parameters cost a fetch.** The fetched page is cached as the site
returned it, and every local view is derived from it, so these are free even
when they change: `limit`, `include_abstract`, `sort_by` / `local_sort`,
`min_citations`, `min_impact_factor`, `sources_only`, `fields`. These are a
different request and cost a fetch: `query`, `channel`, `site_sort`, `page`,
`year_from` / `year_to`, `exclude_ut`.

The older names `sort` and `sort_by` still work and mean the same thing; the
new names say which one is which.

`fields` projects each record to the listed keys (plus `url`, which `detail`
needs). `include_abstract` on 25 rows is tens of kilobytes; most callers want
a title, a year and a DOI.

`count_only` drops `records` entirely and returns the count plus the
diagnostics that explain it. Testing whether an expression parses and matches
anything should not cost a full page of context: the recorded advice was
`limit: 1, fields: ["title"]`, which still returns a record.

page.description: Page of the site's own result list. **Reach for `exclude_ut` first on Web of Science** — see below. Use `page` when a channel has no exclusion field (CNKI), or when you need a few more records and the query is already narrow. Each turn re-submits the search and opens the next page, so it is not a way to walk a large result set.
page.title: Page

exclude_ut.description: Records to leave out, by UT identifier (Web of Science only). Use it to hide records you already have, not to go deeper: `records_from`/`records_to` read a range straight out of one export. Each call is an independent request and the set shrinks predictably (38 records, exclude 5 → total 33). `page` still exists for channels without an exclusion field.
exclude_ut.title: Exclude Ut

records_from.description: First record to read, 1-based. Use it with `records_to` to read 1000 hits from one export instead of twenty fifty-record pages: `records_from=1, records_to=1000`, then `records_from=1001`. One export carries at most 1000 — the site allows 1000, but a bigger file misses the 15 s a single action may wait for its download (ADR 0024). `total` stays null for a range read: an export says how many records it carries, not how many the query matched. Mutually exclusive with `page`.
records_from.title: Records From

records_to.description: Last record to read, inclusive. Defaults to `records_from` when only the start is given.
records_to.title: Records To

items.description: A record field to keep. `url` and the quota pair are always kept.

fields.description: Keep only these keys. `url` and the quota pair are always kept, so a projected record can still be followed.
fields.title: Fields

tools.name: detail
tools.description:
Fetch full metadata for one record.

`url` may be either the URL `search` returned, or a bare DOI such as
`10.13841/j.cnki.jxsj.2026.11.001`. CNKI detail URLs are several hundred
characters of encrypted signature — this one has no parameters but `v=` —
so passing them back verbatim is easy to truncate. A DOI is short, stable and
already in every record.

**`include_abstract` defaults to false**, matching `search`: a CNKI abstract
runs about 1200 characters and a WoS one about 1000, which is most of what a
detail response weighs. A caller that wants the volume, issue, pages and DOI
should not pay for text it will not read. `fields` projects the rest, and
always keeps `url` so the record stays followable.

A DOI costs one extra search to resolve into a URL, because that is the only
way to reach the detail page. A URL that is already cached costs nothing.

`channel` is optional: it is inferred from the URL's host, or from the DOI
prefix. Pass it only to override that inference.

items.description: A record field to keep. `url` and the quota pair are always kept.

fields.description: Keep only these keys. `url` and the quota pair are always kept, so a projected record can still be followed.
fields.title: Fields

tools.name: detail_many
tools.description:
Fetch several records in one call.

Each lookup costs the same as `detail` and they run in sequence on purpose:
the policy layer serialises network actions anyway, so firing them in
parallel would only queue them while each held a timeout budget.

`include_abstract` and `fields` behave as in `detail`. A batch of twelve
abstracts is roughly 14 KB, so the default is off here too — this is the call
that most needs it, since the cost multiplies by the batch size.

A failure on one record does not abandon the rest — the response is
`{"results": [{"url", "ok", "record"|"error"}], "ok_count", "failed_count"}`,
so a caller can retry just the ones that failed.

**A risk block is the exception**: it stops the batch. `detail` returns a
`status: "blocked"` payload rather than raising, so this loop used to file it
under `ok: true` and carry on — reporting a batch as successful while the
site was asking the caller to stop. AGENTS.md requires stopping on a block,
and a batch that keeps visiting after one is exactly the behaviour that rule
exists to prevent.

items.description: A record field to keep. `url` and the quota pair are always kept.

fields.description: Keep only these keys on each record. `url` and the quota pair are always kept.
fields.title: Fields

tools.name: export
tools.description:
Render records as RIS or EndNote text.

With `out_path`, the text is written there and **not** returned: a caller
that wants 143 records on disk should not have to pull them through its
context to do it. Without it, the text comes back inline as before.

`include_abstract` defaults to false here even though the records may carry
one. An `AB` field roughly quadruples an RIS entry, and an export is usually
for a reference manager, which fetches abstracts on its own.

tools.name: page_read
tools.description:
Open a publisher article page and say whether it holds the full text.

Give `doi` (preferred — it also decides the publisher) or an article `url`. The
browser opens that address directly, then saves the page as MHTML; the navigation plus the
capture is charged per action that runs — **2** units normally, and a challenge wall is
charged only for the navigation(s) that ran (**1**, or 2 when the build opens the
publisher's home page first), because nothing is captured then.

Read `full_text` first: it is `true` only when the article body was actually read. When it
is `false`, `full_text_reason` says why — `paywall`, `pdf_only`, `abstract_only`,
`doi_not_found`, `unsupported_site` or `blocked` — and **none of those is proof that this
browser lacks institutional access**. `status` keeps its older meanings:

* `ok` — `mhtml_path` holds the article; call `page2md` with it;
* `no_html` — the page holds no article body; `reason` narrows it (`paywall`,
  `abstract_only`, `pdf_only`, `doi_not_found`), and `pdf_url` may offer the PDF route;
* `unsupported_site` — the DOI belongs to a publisher this build does not visit
  (the curated list is in `core/publishers.py`, ADR 0019), so nothing was opened;
* `blocked` — the site showed a human-verification wall. It is recognized from the
  tab title right after the navigation, so **the wall is never captured or saved**
  (ADR 0004): `mhtml_path` is null. Ask the user to solve it in that browser window,
  then call `page_read` again: with the wall solved the article is read from the tab
  that is already open, without navigating and without charge. `snapshot` also works
  for free, but it captures whichever tab is in front.

Nothing is clicked or typed, and a page that only shows a preview is reported as
such rather than passed off as the article.

`refresh: true` ignores a cached capture and navigates again — use it when the caller has
independent evidence the cached verdict is wrong (the reader can see the article in that
window). It costs another navigation, so it is off by default.

tools.name: snapshot
tools.description:
Save the page the user has open as MHTML — one file with its images and CSS.

This is the "read this paper" entry point for pages outside the two channels:
the user opens the article in the browser, `snapshot` writes
`wensu-pages/<title> [<host>] <time>.mhtml` into the download folder, and
`page2md` turns that file into Markdown.

It issues no request of its own — it reads the tab that is already open — so it
spends **no quota** and is not limited to the channel domains. `status` still
reports `bridge_ready`; a false value means the extension is not connected.

tools.name: page2md
tools.description:
Turn a page saved by `page_read` or `snapshot` into Markdown an agent can read.

Runs **inside the server**: no command line, no permission to provision, **0
quota**. `out_dir` defaults to `md/` beside the saved page.

Answers `page_md` (full text with headings, tables and formulae), `index_json` (the
paper as a map: per-section points, key sentences, and each number with the sentence
it came from), plus `engine`, `math_engine` and `warnings`. Read `warnings` first —
they name the places where fidelity was lost (formulae that did not convert, images
that were missing), which is what should trigger "open the PDF" advice.

tools.name: status
tools.description:
Session state: channels, cooldown, quota, bridge readiness.

`brief` returns `version`, `bridge_ready`, `bridge_last_seen`, `quota_remaining`,
`cooldown_until`, and the two extension fields (`extension_version`,
`extension_version_mismatch`) — the cheapest way to see whether the build that
answers is the build that was installed. The full payload is about 500 tokens, more
than a search, and three of its blocks — `channel_capabilities`,
`detail_capabilities`, `action_cost` — are static. Poll `brief` while planning and
read the full answer once.
